<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Michael Arbel
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">David Salinas
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>ELLIS Institute Tübingen
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Frank Hutter
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>University of Freiburg
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>ELLIS Institute Tübingen
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>PriorLabs<sup id="id1" class="ltx_sup">*</sup>Equal contribution
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author"><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>INRIA
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent foundational models for tabular data, such as TabPFN, excel at adapting to new tasks via in-context learning, but remain constrained to a fixed, pre-defined number of target dimensions—often necessitating costly ensembling strategies. We trace this constraint to a deeper architectural shortcoming: these models lack target equivariance, so that permuting target dimension orderings alters their predictions. This deficiency gives rise to an irreducible “equivariance gap,” an error term that introduces instability in predictions. We eliminate this gap by designing a fully target-equivariant architecture—ensuring permutation invariance via equivariant encoders, decoders, and a bi-attention mechanism. Empirical evaluation on standard classification benchmarks shows that, on datasets with more classes than those seen during pre-training, our model matches or surpasses existing methods while incurring lower computational overhead.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Tabular data, a prevalent format in many real-world applications, has historically presented unique challenges to deep learning due to its lack of inherent structure compared to image or text data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>.
Foundation models, such as TabPFN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>, have recently been introduced to tackle classification tasks in tabular domains. These models leverage <em id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">in-context learning</em> capabilities of transformers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>, to perform both training and prediction in a single model evaluation, without requiring any parameter updates, achieving remarkable performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">At the core of these foundational models is a pre-training procedure in which a transformer model is trained to predict test targets from test covariates, conditioned on training covariate/target pairs all of which are randomly sampled from some well-designed generative model. While it might seem surprising, at first, how a model pre-trained on synthetic data could perform well on real unseen data, recent work, such as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nagler [26]</a></cite>, provides a theoretical study that shades some light on this phenomenon. These models, leverage the transformer architecture to perform <em id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">attention over rows</em>—attending to all samples simultaneously to enable cross-sample comparison.
Applying attention over rows is crucial, as it enables the model to capture higher-order similarities between samples while preserving an inherent symmetry of tabular data—namely, that row order is irrelevant under the common i.i.d. assumption in supervised learning.
Conveniently, such a mechanism also allows, in theory, handling an arbitrary number of training samples—a property that enables the model to generalize across tasks with varying dataset sizes without architectural modifications.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">However, models such as TabPFN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> are inherently confined to covariate–target pairs of fixed, predefined dimension, thereby limiting their applicability to datasets that match these specifications. This limitation can be alleviated via additional data pre<span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text">-</span>processing—e.g., projecting high<span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text">-</span>dimensional covariates into a lower<span id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text">-</span>dimensional subspace—or by post<span id="S1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text">-</span>processing model predictions,—e.g. employing hierarchical strategies for classification tasks with many classes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>. However, the increased computational burden often offsets some of the benefits offered by <em id="S1.p3.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">in-context learning</em>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Recent work in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite> have partially addressed these challenges, allowing the model to handle arbitrary number of covariates, albeit, requiring the target dimension to have a fixed pre-defined dimension.
A key insight there, is to exploit another inherent symmetry of tabular data: the arrangement of columns/covariates’s dimensions should not influence model predictions. This is achieved through the bi-attention mechanism which alternates between attention over samples/rows and <em id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">columns</em>, i.e. covariates dimensions, thereby making the model equivariant to feature permutations just as it is equivariant to sample permutations.
Nevertheless, these models remain limited to tasks where the target size matches the predefined dimensionality.
While covariates are provided for both training and test samples, only training targets are available to the model. This asymmetry between training and test samples complicates direct extensions of the above approaches to handle the targets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we propose EquiTabPFN, a novel architecture that enforces target equivariance, thus ensuring more robust and consistent predictions while handling targets of arbitrary dimensions.
Unlike feature equivariance which can be directly obtained using a bi-attention mechanism, we achieve target equivariance by carefully combining three different mechanisms:
(1) Bi-attention across covariates/target components and datapoints,
(2) Prediction tokens to replace unavailable test targets, and
(3) A non-parametric decoder preserving equivariance in predictions.
We then establish the importance of target equivariance through theoretical and empirical analyses.
In our theoretical study, we show that optimal functions for the pre-training procedure must necessarily be target-equivariant. Finally, we demonstrate, on real-world datasets, that target-equivariant models are beneficial both in terms of classification performance and inference runtime.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Prior-Fitted Networks.</span> Since the introduction of TabPFN in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hollmann et al. [12]</a></cite>, which demonstrates how such a model can be successfully trained on synthetic data,
several works have leveraged this architecture for applications such as Bayesian Optimization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>, forecasting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>, learning curve extrapolation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>, and fairness analysis <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>. Aside from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hollmann et al. [13]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Müller et al. [24]</a></cite> that proposed a covariate equivariant version of the TabPFN models to better capture natural symmetries of tabular data,
other works focused on improving scalability and speed of the model. This includes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Müller et al. [22]</a></cite> who proposed to pre-train the model for producing the weights on an MLP by in-context learning, so that the resulting MLP performs well on a test portion of a particular dataset while achieving much lower latency.
Recently, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qu et al. [27]</a></cite> improved the scalability w.r.t. to the sample size by introducing a two-stage architecture that first builds fixed-dimensional embeddings of rows, followed by a transformer for efficient in-context learning. All these approaches, still require a pre-defined fixed target dimension.
The focus is orthogonal to ours, as we specifically analyze and enhance the target’s representation of TabPFN family of architectures.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Modifying Prior-Fitted Networks outputs.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To the best of our knowledge, no previous approach has proposed a <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">target-equivariant</em> architecture for foundational tabular models, with the exception of the concurrent work from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koshil et al. [16]</a></cite> which unlike us avoid to process labels with non-linear outputs to focus on interpretability versus accuracy.
Several works have also proposed modifications to the output architecture of TabPFN. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Müller et al. [24]</a></cite> introduced a modification of the output, replacing the linear projection from token embeddings to the target with Generalized Additive Models.
This approach improves the interpretability of the model by constructing shape functions for each feature, which can be analyzed independently. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Margeloiu et al. [19]</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ye et al. [36]</a></cite> explored combining non-parametric models on top of TabPFN. Both approaches require training a model at inference time unlike our method.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Beyond pre-defined target dimensionality.</span>
To address TabPFN’s limitation to a predefined number of classes, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hollmann et al. [13]</a></cite> propose to split the classification problem into smaller ones on which the model can be employed, then to aggregate predictions using a strategy, such as the one based on an error-correcting output codes (ECOC) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>. In this work, we show that such a strategy results in an increased computational cost compared to using our architecture that is natively target equivariant.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qu et al. [27]</a></cite> proposed to use a hierarchical classification strategy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite> which still incurs an increased computational cost. Recently, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu and Bergman [35]</a></cite> propose a mechanism to handle arbitrary number of classes without target equivariance and require a different paradigm involving an adversarial training procedure.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Equivariance beyond tabular methods.</span>
Designing equivariant architectures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite> has long been recognized as beneficial, with the most prominent example being convolutional neural networks, which are equivariant to image translation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite>. More recently, research has focused on designing architectures with other symmetries, such as those present in spherical <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>, set <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite>, or graph data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>. Recent work has also explored incorporating symmetries in Large Language Models. For instance, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Egressy and Stühmer [8]</a></cite> proposed a modification to self-attention that produces outputs equivariant to permutations of multiple-choice options, ensuring that the order of choices does not affect the result—a property known to be important in LLM applications such as LLM judges <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Background on Prior-Fitted Networks</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hollmann et al. [12]</a></cite> introduced a pre-trained model, TabPFN, that leverages the transformer architecture <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite> to perform <em id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">in-context learning</em> on unseen tabular datasets for classification tasks without the need for any further training.
Specifically, given training and test datasets of input-output pairs <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X,Y):=(x_{n},y_{n})_{n=1}^{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>:=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(X,Y):=(x_{n},y_{n})_{n=1}^{N}</annotation></semantics></math> and test samples <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X^{\star},Y^{\star}):=(x_{m}^{\star},y^{\star})_{m=1}^{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>Y</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>:=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>m</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(X^{\star},Y^{\star}):=(x_{m}^{\star},y^{\star})_{m=1}^{M}</annotation></semantics></math>, TabPFN returns a prediction <math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{Y}=f_{X,Y}\left(X^{\star}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{Y}=f_{X,Y}\left(X^{\star}\right)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{X,Y}\left(X^{\star}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{X,Y}\left(X^{\star}\right)</annotation></semantics></math> is the output of the network when provided with the training collection <math id="S3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X,Y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(X,Y)</annotation></semantics></math> and test queries <math id="S3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math>. Here the input vectors <math id="S3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{n}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{m}^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>m</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{m}^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> belong to a euclidean space <math id="S3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>p</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{p}</annotation></semantics></math>, while classes are represented by one-hot vectors <math id="S3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>q</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{q}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We now briefly describe the three modules of TabPFN model: an encoder, a backbone and a decoder, as it will help identify the main architectural constrains that impose a limit on the number of classes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Linear Encoder. </span> The encoder module constructs training and test tokens <math id="S3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(e_{n})_{n=1}^{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(e_{n})_{n=1}^{N}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(e^{\star}_{m})_{m=1}^{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>e</mi><mi>m</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(e^{\star}_{m})_{m=1}^{M}</annotation></semantics></math> that are provided to the transformer backbone assuming the inputs <math id="S3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> are vectors of fixed dimensions <math id="S3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{max}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Each training token <math id="S3.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{n}</annotation></semantics></math> is obtained by linearly embedding both covariate <math id="S3.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{n}</annotation></semantics></math> and target <math id="S3.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{n}</annotation></semantics></math> into a feature space of fixed dimension <math id="S3.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> and then summing both embeddings, i.e. <math id="S3.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{n}=Ux_{n}+Vy_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{n}=Ux_{n}+Vy_{n}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>U</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math> are trainable matrices of sizes <math id="S3.p3.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d\times p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d\times p</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p3.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d\times q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d\times q</annotation></semantics></math>. On the other hand, the test token consists only in embedding the test covariate <math id="S3.p3.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{\star}_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>m</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{\star}_{m}</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e. <math id="S3.p3.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e^{\star}_{m}=Ux_{m}^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>e</mi><mi>m</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>m</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^{\star}_{m}=Ux_{m}^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> since the test target <math id="S3.p3.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{\star}_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>m</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{\star}_{m}</annotation></semantics></math> is not provided to the network. While targets with smaller dimensions can be handled by a simple zero-padding procedure (see <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hollmann et al. [12]</a></cite>), the encoder cannot easily accommodate target data with dimensions greater than <math id="S3.p3.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Transformer backbone.</span> The backbone consists of a succession of residual multi-head self-attention layers between all tokens followed by a residual feed-forward network applied to each token.
In order to avoid information leakage from test to train data, an attention mask ensures that all tokens can only attend to the training tokens. This also ensures that test tokens are processed independently from each other.
The residual connections in the backbone preserve the initial feature dimension <math id="S3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>, so that each token is still associated to a particular sample while gradually incorporating information from all training tokens.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MLP decoder.</span> The decoder consists of a one-hidden layer MLP that takes each test output token <math id="S3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e^{\star}_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>e</mi><mi>m</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^{\star}_{m}</annotation></semantics></math> produced by the transformer backbone and produces a prediction vector <math id="S3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{y}_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>m</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{y}_{m}</annotation></semantics></math> of dimension <math id="S3.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math>.
As the decoder requires a pre-defined target dimension <math id="S3.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math>, it cannot be used post-hoc on new data with higher target dimensions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">A notable property of the TabPFN architecture is its invariance of the test predictions to the order by which training and test points are provided.
This property is desirable since the order of training points is arbitrary and should not influence predictions on test samples.
However, the network lacks <em id="S3.p6.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">equivariance</em> w.r.t. the targets’ dimensions, meaning that predictions are highly dependent on the order by which the training target dimensions are provided, an undesirable property as we show in our theoretical analysis in <a href="#S5" title="5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Target equivariant prior-fitted network</h2>

<figure id="S4.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2502.06684v4/architecture.png" id="S4.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:471/184;" width="471" height="184" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S4.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Overview of EquiTabPFN’s architecture.
Data is tokenized via an encoder, processed using self-attention, and decoded to obtain predictions. The encoder maps each covariate to a single token and embeds target components into tokens via a <math id="S4.F1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\times 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\times 1</annotation></semantics></math> convolution.
Missing test tokens are replaced by prediction tokens.
Self-attention alternates between (1) feature-wise attention, with target tokens attending only to covariate tokens (gray arrows) while covariate tokens attend to all tokens (blue arrows); (2) Data-wise attention, where test tokens attend only to training tokens (blue arrows), and training tokens attend to themselves (gray arrows).</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce EquiTabPFN, a new model architecture for in-context learning on tabular data, that is permutation equivariant w.r.t. the target’s components.
Our architecture integrates self-attention mechanisms across data points and data components to leverage relationships between datapoints while preserving equivariance by processing individual attributes (such as the targets components).
Unlike TabPFN which requires fixed target dimensions for all datasets, EquiTabPFN allows the dimensions of the target to change depending on the dataset as a consequence of its equivariant architecture.
EquiTabPFN consists of three major modules: a target equivariant encoder, an attention module both across data components and across data points, and a non-parametric equivariant decoder, each designed to facilitate the end-to-end learning of components interactions and datapoint relationships, see <a href="#S4.F1" title="In 4 Target equivariant prior-fitted network ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
Below, we elaborate on each module and their interactions.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Target equivariant encoder</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The encoder constructs training and test tokens by applying a linear projection to both covariates and targets so that target equivariance is preserved.
Specifically, following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>, each training and test covariate vector <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{n}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{\star}_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>m</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{\star}_{m}</annotation></semantics></math> is encoded into a single token of dimension <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> by applying a linear projection matrix <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>U</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U</annotation></semantics></math> of size <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d\times p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d\times p</annotation></semantics></math>.
However, instead of adding a linear projection of the training targets to each corresponding training token, as done in the case of TabPFN (see <a href="#S3" title="3 Background on Prior-Fitted Networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>), we compute a token for each component <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(y_{n})_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(y_{n})_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> of a training target by multiplying them with an embedding vector <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math> of dimension <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> for all <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\leq j\leq q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\leq j\leq q</annotation></semantics></math>. This operation amounts to applying a <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\times 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\times 1</annotation></semantics></math> convolution along the components of each target which preserves target equivariance.
Since, the validation target <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>Y</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> is not provided to the model as input, it is replaced by a trainable <em id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">prediction token</em> <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\text{pred}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mtext>pred</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\text{pred}}</annotation></semantics></math> of dimension <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> that is repeated <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\times q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\times q</annotation></semantics></math> times to form an initial guess <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{Y}^{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>Y</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{Y}^{0}</annotation></semantics></math> of the target.
When considering a batch <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{B}</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> datasets <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="((X,Y),(X^{\star},Y^{\star}))\in\mathcal{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>Y</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">((X,Y),(X^{\star},Y^{\star}))\in\mathcal{B}</annotation></semantics></math> of same dimensions,
all these embeddings along with prediction tokens are collected to form a single tensor <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math> of shape <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(B,N+M,q+1,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(B,N+M,q+1,d)</annotation></semantics></math>. Here, for each batch element <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="((X,Y),(X^{\star},Y^{\star}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>Y</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">((X,Y),(X^{\star},Y^{\star}))</annotation></semantics></math> of index <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math>, the blocks <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m23" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="E_{b,:N,1,:}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mo rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>:</mo></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{b,:N,1,:}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m24" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="E_{b,N:M,1,:}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>:</mo></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{b,N:M,1,:}</annotation></semantics></math> correspond to embeddings of <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m25" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m27" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="E_{b,:N,1:q,:}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mo rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>:</mo></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{b,:N,1:q,:}</annotation></semantics></math> represents the embedding of <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m28" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y</annotation></semantics></math> while <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m29" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="E_{b,N:M,1:q,:}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>:</mo></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{b,N:M,1:q,:}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the initial guess <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m30" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{Y}^{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>Y</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{Y}^{0}</annotation></semantics></math> obtained using the prediction token. This tensor is then processed by the attention modules as described next.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Self-Attention Mechanisms</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The core of the architecture involves two alternating self-attention modules: self-attention across components <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{SelfAtt}_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">SelfAtt</mtext><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{SelfAtt}_{c}</annotation></semantics></math> and self-attention across datapoints <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{SelfAtt}_{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">SelfAtt</mtext><mi>b</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{SelfAtt}_{b}</annotation></semantics></math> used for transforming the tokens. These alternating self-attention layers allow the model to learn both intra-samples components interactions and inter-samples relationships. Following standard design choices for transformers, we apply residual connections and layer normalization to ensure stability and robust gradient flow, i.e.:</p>
<table id="S4.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.Ex1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle E</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\leftarrow\text{LN}\left(E+\textbf{SelfAtt}_{c/b}(E)\right)," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mtext>LN</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">SelfAtt</mtext><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\leftarrow\text{LN}\left(E+\textbf{SelfAtt}_{c/b}(E)\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle E</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\leftarrow\text{LN}\left(E+\text{MLP}(E)\right)," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mtext>LN</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mtext>MLP</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\leftarrow\text{LN}\left(E+\text{MLP}(E)\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <span id="S4.SS2.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LN</span> denotes the layer normalization layer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>, <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{SelfAtt}_{c/b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">SelfAtt</mtext><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{SelfAtt}_{c/b}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes one of the considered self-attention mechanisms and <span id="S4.SS2.p1.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MLP</span> is a one hidden-layer network acting on each embedding independently. Below, we describe both self-attention mechanisms in more detail.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Self-attention across components</span> allows interactions among components within each datapoint.
It is applied independently per samples to preserve equivariance w.r.t. to the samples. In practice, this is achieved by reshaping the activation into a tensor of the shape <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(B\times(N+M),q+1,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(B\times(N+M),q+1,d)</annotation></semantics></math> before applying attention between <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q+1</annotation></semantics></math> covariate tokens of dimension <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>. We further employ a masking strategy that we found useful empirically: forcing target tokens to attend only to the covariate token, while allowing the covariate token to attend to all tokens.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Self-Attention across datapoints</span> captures relationships between datapoint embeddings, allowing the model to aggregate information globally.
It is applied between samples and independently per each input dimensions <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> to preserve equivariance. In practice, this is achieved by reshaping the activation into a tensor of the shape <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(B\times(q+1),N+M,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(B\times(q+1),N+M,d)</annotation></semantics></math> before applying attention between <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N+M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N+M</annotation></semantics></math> training and validation tokens of dimension <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>. Similarly to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>, training and validation tokens only attend to training tokens.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Remark.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">EquiTabPFN and TabPFN both have linear computational complexity in the number of classes, but EquiTabPFN has a larger factor due to self-attention across components.
In TabPFN, linear scaling arises from projecting classes into a fixed-dimensional space and then mapping back fixed dimensional features to classes, while the backbone remains independent of the number of classes.
In contrast, EquiTabPFN’s backbone scales linearly with class number, allowing it to handle arbitrary class counts.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Non-parametric equivariant decoder</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The decoder aggregates the processed embeddings to produce prediction <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{Y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>Y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{Y}</annotation></semantics></math>. This is achieved in two steps: an attention module first computes an intermediate prediction <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{Y}=(\tilde{y}_{m})_{m=1}^{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Y</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{Y}=(\tilde{y}_{m})_{m=1}^{M}</annotation></semantics></math> in the form of a weighted average of training targets <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y</annotation></semantics></math>, then a residual correction is added to produce the final prediction.
More precisely, the attention module uses the embeddings of the training and validation samples as keys and queries, while the attention values are simply the training targets <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e.
<math id="S4.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{y}_{m}=\sum_{n=1}^{N}y_{n}\text{SoftMax}\left(\sum_{i,u}E_{b,n,i,u}E_{b,m,i,u}/\sqrt{(1+q)d}\right)," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>m</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>SoftMax</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo lspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><msqrt><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{y}_{m}=\sum_{n=1}^{N}y_{n}\text{SoftMax}\left(\sum_{i,u}E_{b,n,i,u}E_{b,m,i,u}/\sqrt{(1+q)d}\right),</annotation></semantics></math>
where <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> is the batch-index corresponding to the training target <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y</annotation></semantics></math>.
The residual correction, in the form of a point-wise MLP, operates independently on each dimension <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> of the attention output <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{y}_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>m</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{y}_{m}</annotation></semantics></math> so that equivariance is preserved while enabling nonlinear interactions between training values.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Without the residual correction and removing the dependence of the keys and queries embeddings on the training targets <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y</annotation></semantics></math> (for instance by setting the weights of the target encoder and pointwise MLP to <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math>), the decoder becomes a <span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">linear non-parametric regression estimator</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>, Definition 1.7]</cite>, which is a generalization of Nadaraya-Watson’s estimator
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite>.
However, linear estimators are known to be suboptimal compared to non-linear ones <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>. This motivates introducing a nonlinear dependence of the estimator to <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y</annotation></semantics></math>, in our setting, to increase the expressiveness of the decoder allowing it to adapt to the prediction task at hand. Experimentally, we also found a clear improvement when adding such a residual correction and making the embeddings dependent on the targets.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Pre-training Procedure</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">EquiTabPFN can be pre-trained using the same procedure as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hollmann et al. [12]</a></cite>, on artificial datasets sampled from a sophisticated generative model meant to capture the real-world distribution of datasets.
More precisely, each artificial dataset consists of training/and test splits <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X,Y):=(x_{n},y_{n})_{n=1}^{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>:=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(X,Y):=(x_{n},y_{n})_{n=1}^{N}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X^{\star},Y^{\star}):=(x_{m}^{\star},y_{m}^{\star})_{m=1}^{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>Y</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>:=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>m</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mi>m</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(X^{\star},Y^{\star}):=(x_{m}^{\star},y_{m}^{\star})_{m=1}^{M}</annotation></semantics></math> sampled according to a conditional distribution <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(x,y|\psi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>ψ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(x,y|\psi)</annotation></semantics></math> characterized by a <em id="S4.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">latent</em> parameter <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math>. The parameter <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math> characterizes the dataset and is itself sampled according to a predefined prior <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(\psi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ψ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\psi)</annotation></semantics></math>. The pre-training procedure requires repeatedly generating artificial datasets and training the model to predict test target values <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>Y</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> given corresponding test covariates <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> as well as training covariates/target pairs <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X,Y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(X,Y)</annotation></semantics></math> by minimizing an objective of the form:</p>
<table id="S4.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.E1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(f):=\mathbb{E}\left[\ell\left(f_{X,Y}\left(X^{\star}\right),Y^{\star}\right)\right]." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>Y</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(f):=\mathbb{E}\left[\ell\left(f_{X,Y}\left(X^{\star}\right),Y^{\star}\right)\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Here, <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(y,y^{\prime})\mapsto\ell(y,y^{\prime})\in\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">↦</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(y,y^{\prime})\mapsto\ell(y,y^{\prime})\in\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math> is a point-wise loss, typically cross-entropy, and the expectation is over the collections datasets sampled according to the dataset prior. Note that each test query <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{m}^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>m</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{m}^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> is processed independently by the network <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> so that <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{X,Y}\left(X^{\star}\right)=(f_{X,Y}\left(x_{m}^{\star}\right))_{m=1}^{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>m</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{X,Y}\left(X^{\star}\right)=(f_{X,Y}\left(x_{m}^{\star}\right))_{m=1}^{M}</annotation></semantics></math>. Next, we show, under natural conditions, that target equivariant functions constitute the right space of functions when searching for solutions to objectives of the form in <a href="#S4.E1" title="In 4.4 Pre-training Procedure ‣ 4 Target equivariant prior-fitted network ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Equation</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now formally analyze the impact of non-target equivariance on the training objective. We begin by precisely defining target equivariance, then show that an optimal solution must be equivariant or otherwise incurs an error quantified by the <em id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">target equivariance gap</em>. Finally, through empirical analysis of TabPFN training, we illustrate how the equivariance gap decreases slowly, highlighting the fundamental challenge non-equivariant architectures face in learning this key data symmetry.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Optimality of target equivariant networks</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">When presenting a new unseen dataset of covariate/target pairs <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x_{n},y_{n})_{n=1}^{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x_{n},y_{n})_{n=1}^{N}</annotation></semantics></math> to a pre-trained model, the order of the component’s target is arbitrary.
In other words, given target vectors of the form <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{n}=\left((y_{n})_{1},\dots,(y_{n})_{q}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{n}=\left((y_{n})_{1},\dots,(y_{n})_{q}\right)</annotation></semantics></math>, these could as well be presented in a different order by applying a permutation <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> to the components of <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{n}</annotation></semantics></math> to obtain a permuted target <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma(y_{n})=\left((y_{n})_{\sigma(1)},\dots,(y_{n})_{\sigma(q)}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma(y_{n})=\left((y_{n})_{\sigma(1)},\dots,(y_{n})_{\sigma(q)}\right)</annotation></semantics></math>.
The transformed dataset <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x_{n},\sigma(y_{n}))_{n=1}^{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x_{n},\sigma(y_{n}))_{n=1}^{N}</annotation></semantics></math> is still essentially the same as the original dataset up to the permutation as we only changed the order of the target components. For instance, when the target represents a one hot encoding vector of <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math> classes: "red" or "blue", it should not matter whether we encode "red" as the first or the second class in the one-hot vector.
Consequently, a pre-trained model should be able to provide consistent predictions regardless of the component’s order.
More formally, the model should satisfy the following equivariance property:</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S5.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 5.1</span></span><span id="S5.Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Target permutation equivariance)<span id="S5.Thmtheorem1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S5.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A function <math id="S5.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is permutation <em id="S5.Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_upright">equivariant</em> in the targets’ components iff for any training data <math id="S5.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X,Y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(X,Y)</annotation></semantics></math> and test covariates <math id="S5.Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math>:</span></p>
<table id="S5.EGx3" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S5.E2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S5.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\forall\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{q},\quad\sigma^{-1}\left(f_{X,\sigma(Y)}\left(X^{*}\right)\right)=f_{X,Y}\left(X^{*}\right)," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>σ</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>𝔖</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\forall\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{q},\quad\sigma^{-1}\left(f_{X,\sigma(Y)}\left(X^{*}\right)\right)=f_{X,Y}\left(X^{*}\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.Thmtheorem1.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.Thmtheorem1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">where <math id="S5.Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathfrak{S}_{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝔖</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathfrak{S}_{q}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the set of all possible permutations of the components of a vector of <math id="S5.Thmtheorem1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> elements.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">It is clear from <a href="#S5.Thmtheorem1" title="Definition 5.1 (Target permutation equivariance). ‣ 5.1 Optimality of target equivariant networks ‣ 5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Definition</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.1</span></a> that EquiTabPFN is target equivariant. Even when a model is not target equivariant by construction, it is natural to expect it to learn to be target equivariant, when trained via the objective in <a href="#S4.E1" title="In 4.4 Pre-training Procedure ‣ 4 Target equivariant prior-fitted network ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Equation</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> over a large class of randomly sampled datasets.
To formalize this, we define the <em id="S5.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">target equivariance gap</em>, which quantifies the deviation of a function <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> from its symmetrized counterpart <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{f}^{\text{equi}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>f</mi><mtext>equi</mtext></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{f}^{\text{equi}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.Thmtheorem2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S5.Thmtheorem2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 5.2</span></span><span id="S5.Thmtheorem2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Target-equivariance gap)<span id="S5.Thmtheorem2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S5.Thmtheorem2.p1" class="ltx_para">
