<p id="S5.Thmtheorem2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.Thmtheorem2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The target-equivariance gap <math id="S5.Thmtheorem2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}^{\text{equi}}(f)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">equi</mtext></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}^{\text{equi}}(f)</annotation></semantics></math> of a function <math id="S5.Thmtheorem2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> w.r.t. to <math id="S5.Thmtheorem2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}</annotation></semantics></math> is the difference between the objective values at <math id="S5.Thmtheorem2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> and its <em id="S5.Thmtheorem2.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_upright">symmetrized</em> version <math id="S5.Thmtheorem2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{f}^{\text{equi}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>f</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">equi</mtext></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{f}^{\text{equi}}</annotation></semantics></math>:</span></p>
<table id="S5.EGx4" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S5.E3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S5.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{E}^{\text{equi}}(f):=\mathcal{L}(f)-\mathcal{L}({f}^{\text{equi}})," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">equi</mtext></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>f</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">equi</mtext></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{E}^{\text{equi}}(f):=\mathcal{L}(f)-\mathcal{L}({f}^{\text{equi}}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.Thmtheorem2.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.Thmtheorem2.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">where <math id="S5.Thmtheorem2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{f}^{\text{equi}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>f</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">equi</mtext></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{f}^{\text{equi}}</annotation></semantics></math> is obtained by applying the following averaging operation w.r.t. to the uniform distribution <math id="S5.Thmtheorem2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}</annotation></semantics></math> over all permutations <math id="S5.Thmtheorem2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> of the target:</span></p>
<table id="S5.EGx5" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S5.E4"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S5.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle{f}^{\text{equi}}_{X,Y}\left(X^{\star}\right)=\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\left[\sigma^{-1}\left(f_{X,\sigma(Y)}\left(X^{\star}\right)\right)\right]." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">equi</mtext></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle{f}^{\text{equi}}_{X,Y}\left(X^{\star}\right)=\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\left[\sigma^{-1}\left(f_{X,\sigma(Y)}\left(X^{\star}\right)\right)\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">By construction, <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{f}^{\text{equi}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>f</mi><mtext>equi</mtext></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{f}^{\text{equi}}</annotation></semantics></math> is permutation equivariant w.r.t. the target components. Moreover it can be easily shown that a function <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is itself equivariant iff <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{f}^{\text{equi}}=f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mtext>equi</mtext></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{f}^{\text{equi}}=f</annotation></semantics></math>, so that the gap vanishes. In general, the equivariance gap can take negative values.
However, we establish later that this equivariance gap must be non-negative under the following assumptions on the pointwise loss <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> and the marginal distribution <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> of the data:</p>
<ol id="S5.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S5.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(<span id="S5.I1.i1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A</span>)</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Invariance and convexity of the pointwise loss.</span> The pointwise loss <math id="S5.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> is strictly convex in its first argument and is invariant to permutations of the components of its arguments, i.e. for any permutation <math id="S5.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>, it holds that: <math id="S5.I1.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell(\sigma(y),\sigma(y^{\prime}))=\ell(y,y^{\prime})." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell(\sigma(y),\sigma(y^{\prime}))=\ell(y,y^{\prime}).</annotation></semantics></math></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(<span id="S5.I1.i2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">B</span>)</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Invariance of the data distribution.</span> The marginal distribution of the data is invariant to permutations applied to <math id="S5.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>Y</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e.:
<math id="S5.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(X,\sigma(Y),X^{\star},\sigma(Y^{\star}))=p(X,Y,X^{\star},Y^{\star})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>Y</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>Y</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(X,\sigma(Y),X^{\star},\sigma(Y^{\star}))=p(X,Y,X^{\star},Y^{\star})</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S5.I1.i1" title="In 5.1 Optimality of target equivariant networks ‣ 5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">(A)</span></a> is satisfied for most commonly used losses such as the cross-entropy loss or the quadratic loss. <a href="#S5.I1.i2" title="In 5.1 Optimality of target equivariant networks ‣ 5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">(B)</span></a> holds as soon as data can be presented without a preferred ordering, as most i.i.d. tabular datasets. The next proposition, proved in <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Proofs ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>, decomposes the objective into a non-negative equivariance gap and an optimality error.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.Thmtheorem3" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_proposition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S5.Thmtheorem3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proposition 5.3</span></span><span id="S5.Thmtheorem3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S5.Thmtheorem3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.Thmtheorem3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.Thmtheorem3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Under <a href="#S5.I1.i1" title="In 5.1 Optimality of target equivariant networks ‣ 5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">(A)</span></a> and <a href="#S5.I1.i2" title="Assumption (B) ‣ 5.1 Optimality of target equivariant networks ‣ 5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">(B)</span></a>, the equivariance gap <math id="S5.Thmtheorem3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}^{\text{equi}}(f)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">equi</mtext></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}^{\text{equi}}(f)</annotation></semantics></math> is always non-negative and only equal to <math id="S5.Thmtheorem3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> when <math id="S5.Thmtheorem3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is equivariant to permutations, so that for any <math id="S5.Thmtheorem3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math>:</span></p>
<table id="S5.EGx6" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S5.Ex2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S5.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(f)=\mathcal{L}({f}^{\text{equi}})+\mathcal{E}^{\text{equi}}(f)\geq\mathcal{L}({f}^{\text{equi}})." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>f</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">equi</mtext></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">equi</mtext></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>f</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">equi</mtext></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(f)=\mathcal{L}({f}^{\text{equi}})+\mathcal{E}^{\text{equi}}(f)\geq\mathcal{L}({f}^{\text{equi}}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.Thmtheorem3.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.Thmtheorem3.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Moreover, if <math id="S5.Thmtheorem3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> is a minimizer of <math id="S5.Thmtheorem3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}</annotation></semantics></math> over all measurable functions, then <math id="S5.Thmtheorem3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> must be target equivariant.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof sketch.</h6>
<div id="S5.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text">The key step is to express the objective as an expectation over permutations using <a href="#S5.I1.i1" title="In 5.1 Optimality of target equivariant networks ‣ 5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">(A)</span></a> and <a href="#S5.I1.i2" title="Assumption (B) ‣ 5.1 Optimality of target equivariant networks ‣ 5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">(B)</span></a> on the data and loss: <math id="S5.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(f)=\mathbb{E}_{p}\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\left[\ell\left(\sigma^{-1}f_{X,\sigma(Y)}\left(X^{\star}\right),Y^{\star}\right)\right]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>Y</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(f)=\mathbb{E}_{p}\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\left[\ell\left(\sigma^{-1}f_{X,\sigma(Y)}\left(X^{\star}\right),Y^{\star}\right)\right]</annotation></semantics></math>. The non-negativity of the equivariance gap is then established using Jensen’s inequality by convexity of the loss <math id="S5.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> in its first argument (<a href="#S5.I1.i1" title="In 5.1 Optimality of target equivariant networks ‣ 5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">(A)</span></a>).
Now, assume by contradiction that <math id="S5.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> is not equivariant and note that <math id="S5.SS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{f^{\star}}^{\text{equi}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mmultiscripts><mi>f</mi><mrow></mrow><mo>⋆</mo><mrow></mrow><mtext>equi</mtext></mmultiscripts><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{f^{\star}}^{\text{equi}}</annotation></semantics></math> is a measurable function by construction.
It follows that <math id="S5.SS1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}^{\text{equi}}(f^{\star})&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mtext>equi</mtext></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}^{\text{equi}}(f^{\star})&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>, which directly implies that <math id="S5.SS1.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(f^{\star})&gt;\mathcal{L}({f^{\star}}^{\text{equi}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mmultiscripts><mi>f</mi><mrow></mrow><mo>⋆</mo><mrow></mrow><mtext>equi</mtext></mmultiscripts><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(f^{\star})&gt;\mathcal{L}({f^{\star}}^{\text{equi}})</annotation></semantics></math>, thus contradicting the optimality of <math id="S5.SS1.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math>.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S5.Thmtheorem3" title="Proposition 5.3. ‣ 5.1 Optimality of target equivariant networks ‣ 5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Proposition</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a> shows that minimizing the objective <math id="S5.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}</annotation></semantics></math> results in a target equivariant function.
Hence, using a non-equivariant model must employ some of its expressive power solely for being equivariant, which can be wasteful, as we verify empirically in <a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Non-equivariance of TabPFNs models ‣ 5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a> below.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Non-equivariance of TabPFNs models</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">PFNs models, as introduced in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hollmann et al. [12]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hollmann et al. [13]</a></cite> are not permutation equivariant in the target’s components. Consequently, they are not guaranteed to provide consistent predictions when the target components are permuted, thus affecting their robustness.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F3" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S5.F3.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_top" style="width:213.9pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.06684v4/boundary-grid.svg" id="S5.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:295/190;" width="295" height="190"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F3.fig1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S5.F3.fig1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Prediction comparison of TabPFN, TabPFN-v2, and our model on the same datasets with three different class orderings (one per column). Models predict on a dense grid using 9 distinct training points, marked with dark crosses, each having a distinct class.
</span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S5.F3.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_top" style="width:120.8pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.06684v4/equivariance-error.svg" id="S5.F3.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:167/175;" width="167" height="175"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F3.fig2.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S5.F3.fig2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Equivariance error for TabPFN observed while training (top) and at inference with different number of classes and ensembles (bottom).

</span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Predictions instabilities.</span> To illustrate the implications of non-equivariance on the robustness of PFNs models, we consider a toy classification problem in <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math> dimensions, where <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">9</annotation></semantics></math> training points are positioned on a <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional regular grid, each corresponding to a different class inspired by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">McCarter [20]</a></cite>. Different pretrained models are then used to predict the classes on a regular grid of <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="40^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>40</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">40^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> points.
<a href="#S5.F3" title="In 5.2 Non-equivariance of TabPFNs models ‣ 5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows the classification boundaries when using the same data but with <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math> different orderings for the classes. It is clear that the ordering heavily affects the prediction even in this simple example, which strongly impacts robustness of models like TabPFN and TabPFN-v2. The predictions of TabPFN-v2 are particularly noisy due to having only 9 training data points which is not an issue in itself, unlike the extreme unstability to the class ordering. Note that the axis are scaled differently for presentation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Target equivariance gap during training.</span> In <a href="#S5.F3" title="In 5.2 Non-equivariance of TabPFNs models ‣ 5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we analyse the equivariance error while training TabPFN.
<a href="#S5.F3" title="In 5.2 Non-equivariance of TabPFNs models ‣ 5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> (left) shows the equivariance error of TabPFN in terms of percentage of violation of <a href="#S5.E2" title="In Definition 5.1 (Target permutation equivariance). ‣ 5.1 Optimality of target equivariant networks ‣ 5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Equation</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, e.g. how frequently the predicted classes <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{X,\sigma(Y)}(X^{*})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{X,\sigma(Y)}(X^{*})</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma\left(f_{X,Y}(X^{*})\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma\left(f_{X,Y}(X^{*})\right)</annotation></semantics></math> differ. We sample 512 datasets from the prior and report standard deviation. In <a href="#S5.F3" title="In 5.2 Non-equivariance of TabPFNs models ‣ 5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> (left), the equivariance error is clear and slowly decreases during training. This non-equivariance 1) induces additional errors for the model as demonstrated in <a href="#S5.Thmtheorem3" title="Proposition 5.3. ‣ 5.1 Optimality of target equivariant networks ‣ 5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Proposition</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a> and 2) causes the model to provide surprising predictions given that permuting the output order can change the results as seen in <a href="#S5.F3" title="In 5.2 Non-equivariance of TabPFNs models ‣ 5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Mitigation via costly ensembling.</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hollmann et al. [12]</a></cite> introduce a mitigation strategy to non-equivariance by averaging several predictions using random permutations of the target dimensions.
Averaging over all possible permutations gives an equivariant function as discussed in <a href="#S5.E4" title="In Definition 5.2 (Target-equivariance gap). ‣ 5.1 Optimality of target equivariant networks ‣ 5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Equation</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. However, this requires making <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(q!)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>!</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(q!)</annotation></semantics></math> calls to the model, where <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of classes. This becomes quickly prohibitive, even for <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q=10</annotation></semantics></math> as considered in the original study.
Randomized estimators, using <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{ens}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{ens}</annotation></semantics></math> random permutations can compute a prediction that converge to the averaged one at a rate of <math id="S5.SS2.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/\sqrt{N_{ens}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msqrt><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/\sqrt{N_{ens}}</annotation></semantics></math>. However, the variance of such estimator would typically present a dependence on the dimension that is, unfortunately, challenging to quantify in general.
This variance is highest when the function is far from being equivariant, constituting the worst scenarios.
We illustrate how fast the model becomes equivariant when using ensembles in <a href="#S5.F3" title="In 5.2 Non-equivariance of TabPFNs models ‣ 5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> (right). While ensembling more permutation helps to make the model <span id="S5.SS2.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">more</span> equivariant, many ensembles are required, in particular, when considering more classes. In contrast, the model we propose is fully target equivariant so that predictions remain the same regardless of the class ordering as illustrated in <a href="#S5.F3" title="In 5.2 Non-equivariance of TabPFNs models ‣ 5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> (bottom).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Experiments</h2>

<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.1 </span>Experimental setup</h3>

<section id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Pretraining.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We trained our model, EquiTabPFN on artificial dataset extending the public code of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Müller et al. [22]</a></cite> and using the same procedure from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hollmann et al. [12]</a></cite> employed to train TabPFNv1. Crucially, it was trained on classification tasks with less than <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math> classes.
The total training time took approximately 4 days on a single A100 GPU with 80GB of memory.
We set our architectures hyperparameters so that they match the number of parameters of previous work, in particular the model we trained contains <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>25M parameters similar to the baselines we consider and we match most our hyperparameters to the same values as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hollmann et al. [12]</a></cite>. We refer to <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Additional Experimental details ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a> for further training details and description of the hyperparameters used.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Benchmarks.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For evaluation, we consider classification tasks from the TabZilla benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>.
To assess the impact of unseen class counts during evaluation (i.e., exceeding <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math>), we consider two setups: one on <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="76" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>76</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">76</annotation></semantics></math> multi-class tasks with at most <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math> classes, and another on <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math> tasks with more than <math id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math> classes.
Details of the datasets/tasks used are provided in <a href="#A2.T1" title="In Appendix B Additional Experimental details ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tables</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and <a href="#A2.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Appendix B Additional Experimental details ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. In all results, except those of <a href="#S6.F5" title="In 6.2 Main results ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> (left), we report the results of EquiTabPFN without ensembling as it is not critical for the performance of our method.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Baselines.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider baselines from the TabZilla benchmark. In addition, we compare with <span id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">TabPFNv2</span>, the state-of-the-art model with open-weights released by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite> and which was shown to out-perform standard baselines, including those appearing in the TabZilla benchmark.
This model was pretrained using an improved prior compared to initial version TabPFNv1. However, the code for the prior and the training is not publicly available. Hence, to allow a fair comparaison, we also include a second version, TabPFNv2<sup id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_sup">∗</sup>, using the exact same architecture as TabPFNv2, but which we trained on the same publicly available prior and training code of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> that we used for our model.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F4" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><img src="2502.06684v4/Tabzilla_box_plot_relative_Accuracy_wrt_KNN_datasets_regular.png" id="S6.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:238/238;" width="238" height="238" alt="Refer to caption"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><img src="2502.06684v4/Tabzilla_box_plot_relative_Accuracy_wrt_KNN_datasets_ood.png" id="S6.F4.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:238/238;" width="238" height="238" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S6.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S6.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Relative improvement over KNN for datasets with less than 10 classes (left) and more than 10 classes (right). Red lines are the median metric over datasets after averaging each dataset over <math id="S6.F4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math> splits. The runtime is displayed with color on a log scale and is reported on a V100 GPU for PFNs. </span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.2 </span>Main results</h3>

<div id="S6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section presents the main experimental findings. Additional results, including ablation of the EquiTabPFN architecture and computational cost comparisons are found in <a href="#A3.SS1" title="C.1 Ablation on the different components of EquiTabPFN. ‣ Appendix C Additional experiment results ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sections</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.1</span></a> and <a href="#A3.SS2" title="C.2 Computational cost comparisons ‣ Appendix C Additional experiment results ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F5" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><img src="2502.06684v4/Tabzilla_pareto_relative_AUC_wrt_KNN_datasets_ood.png" id="S6.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:246/216;" width="246" height="216" alt="Refer to caption"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.06684v4/Tabzilla_efficiency_relative_AUC_wrt_KNN_datasets_ood.svg" id="S6.F5.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:218/216;" width="218" height="216"></object></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S6.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S6.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Left: Scatter plot of runtime vs <math id="S6.F5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo mathsize="1.110em">%</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\%</annotation></semantics></math> AUC improvement over KNN for different methods. Right: barplot of AUC ratio relatively to KNN (blue) and speedup of EquiTabPFN (green).
In both figures, we increase the number of ensembles of TabPFNs variants.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S6.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">EquiTabPFN enables in-context-learning on datasets with unseen class counts.</span> <a href="#S6.F4" title="In Baselines. ‣ 6.1 Experimental setup ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows accuracies relative to the KNN baseline for all models on <math id="S6.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="76" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>76</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">76</annotation></semantics></math> datasets with less than <math id="S6.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math> classes (left) and 10 datasets with more than <math id="S6.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math> classes (right). When considering datasets with more than <math id="S6.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math> classes (right),
EquiTabPFN obtains the best median relative accuracy across all datasets. It strongly outperforms TabPFNv2, which performs worse than a linear model or random forests in terms of relative median. These results show that target-equivariance allows EquiTabPFN to seamlessly generalize to larger numbers of classes even though it was trained on datasets with less than <math id="S6.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math> classes, just like TabPFNv2. Additional evaluations in <a href="#A3.T5" title="In C.4 Critical difference diagrams and performance metric tables ‣ Appendix C Additional experiment results ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tables</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> and <a href="#A3.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ C.4 Critical difference diagrams and performance metric tables ‣ Appendix C Additional experiment results ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> of <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Additional experiment results ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> show that such improvement is consistent over various metrics: AUC, Accuracy and F1 score, for datasets with unseen class counts.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Competitive performance on datasets with class counts seen during pre-training.</span>
On the 76 datasets with less than 10 classes (<a href="#S6.F4" title="In Baselines. ‣ 6.1 Experimental setup ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, left), EquiTabPFN performs comparably to the state-of the art method, TabPFNv2, even though it did not benefit from the improved data prior used in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hollmann et al. [13]</a></cite> as it is not publicly available.
To assess the impact of the pre-training prior on performance, we pre-trained the same network architecture as TabPFNv2 using the same publicly available protocol used for training our method and reported the results for reference (TabPFNv2<sup id="S6.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_sup">∗</sup>). The results show that EquiTabPFN consistently outperforms TabPFNv2<sup id="S6.SS2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_sup">∗</sup> both on dataset with less than <math id="S6.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math> classes and those with unseen class count. These results suggest that EquiTabPFN would likely benefit from the improved training procedure and prior of TabPFNv2.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Speedup over TabPFNv2 on datasets with unseen class counts.</span>
As discussed in <a href="#S3" title="3 Background on Prior-Fitted Networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, PFNs models

cannot natively handle an arbitrary number of classes due to its decoder architecture.
In order to apply TabPFNv2 to problems with more than <math id="S6.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math> classes, we employ the error-correcting output codes (ECOC) strategy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite> as recommended in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hollmann et al. [13]</a></cite>.
Such approach requires decomposing the classification problem into several smaller classification tasks with up to <math id="S6.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math> classes, performing predictions for each sub-task using an ensemble of TabPFNv2 models, at least one model per task, then aggregating predictions using an ECOC strategy.
This incurs an extra computational cost for performing ensembling.
All results reported in <a href="#S6.F4" title="In Baselines. ‣ 6.1 Experimental setup ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> (right) are using the minimal number of ensembles to guarantee coverages of all classes. Despite this sophisticated aggregation strategy, the performance of TabPFNv2 degrades significantly, while still incurring a substantial slow-down compared to EquiTabPFN as shown by the average run-times reported by color in <a href="#S6.F4" title="In Baselines. ‣ 6.1 Experimental setup ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> (left). Note that, for datasets with less than <math id="S6.SS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math> classes (<a href="#S6.F4" title="In Baselines. ‣ 6.1 Experimental setup ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, left) ensembling is not required anymore by TabPFNv2 and the runtime of both methods are comparable.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">EquiTabPFN achieves the best tradeoff between performance and cost on datasets with unseen class counts.</span>
To further illustrate the improved trade-off between runtime and accuracy of our method, we show in <a href="#S6.F5" title="In 6.2 Main results ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> (left) the improvement in AUC relatively to KNN for all methods when both TabPFNv2 and EquiTabPFN are allowed to have more ensembles.
Ensembling generally improves performance of PFN models, as it allows to make more robust predictions by averaging them over transformed version of the datasets, ex: by applying permutations of the labels order as discussed in <a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Non-equivariance of TabPFNs models ‣ 5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>. While ensembling helps improve performance of TabPFNv2, the improvement is marginal compared to EquiTabPFN without ensembling and comes at a considerable computational cost, as also shown in <a href="#S6.F5" title="In 6.2 Main results ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> (right) and on the critical difference diagrams in <a href="#A3.F8" title="In C.4 Critical difference diagrams and performance metric tables ‣ Appendix C Additional experiment results ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figures</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> and <a href="#A3.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ C.4 Critical difference diagrams and performance metric tables ‣ Appendix C Additional experiment results ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> of <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Additional experiment results ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.
Therefore, amongst top performing methods, EquiTabPFN achieves the best trade-off.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Summary.</span> In this paper, we introduced EquiTabPFN, an architecture for PFNs that is equivariant to target permutations and enables in-context learning on datasets with arbitrary class counts.
We established optimality of equivariant architectures for foundational tabular models and proved that non-equivariant models worsens the pre-training objective with an incompressible error term.
Finally, we empirically showed the benefits of EquiTabPFN both in terms of classification performance and inference runtime on synthetic and real-world datasets.
We hope this work enables future developments on prior-fitted networks that incorporate such fundamental symmetry of tabular data.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Non-equivariance.</span>
In some cases, the data may not be target equivariant, for instance on ordinal data. We found only a few of those cases in the benchmarks used (5 of the 86 datasets surveyed). Handling such cases would require to update the prior as it is currently equivariant to target permutation. The method could then be adapted by providing positional embedding or using column indices as input.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Limitations.</span> EquiTabPFN requires a quadratic extra-cost with the number of target dimensions to perform self-attention. While many tabular problems have a relatively small number of target dimensions, this may become a problem for a very large number of dimensions and future work could consider efficient self-attention to address this issue. This may be alleviated by work focused on improving the efficiency of PFNs models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>, <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The code for training and evaluating our model is available at <a href="https://github.com/MichaelArbel/EquiTabPFN/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/MichaelArbel/EquiTabPFN/</a>.</p>
</div>
</section>

<div id="A1.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof of <a href="#S5.Thmtheorem3" title="Proposition 5.3. ‣ 5.1 Optimality of target equivariant networks ‣ 5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Proposition</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a>.</h6>
<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">By <a href="#S5.I1.i2" title="In 5.1 Optimality of target equivariant networks ‣ 5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">(B)</span></a> we can express <math id="A1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}</annotation></semantics></math> as an expectation of the form:</span></p>
<table id="A1.EGx7" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A1.E5"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(f)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(f)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.E5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p}\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\left[\ell\left(f_{X,\sigma(Y)}\left(X^{\star}\right),\sigma(Y^{\star})\right)\right]." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>Y</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p}\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\left[\ell\left(f_{X,\sigma(Y)}\left(X^{\star}\right),\sigma(Y^{\star})\right)\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text">By <a href="#S5.I1.i1" title="In 5.1 Optimality of target equivariant networks ‣ 5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">(A)</span></a>, <math id="A1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> is invariant to permutations, which allows to further write:</span></p>
<table id="A1.EGx8" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A1.E6"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(f)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(f)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.E6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p}\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\left[\ell\left(\sigma^{-1}\left(f_{X,\sigma(Y)}\left(X^{\star}\right)\right),Y^{\star}\right)\right]." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>Y</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p}\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\left[\ell\left(\sigma^{-1}\left(f_{X,\sigma(Y)}\left(X^{\star}\right)\right),Y^{\star}\right)\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text">We will show that <math id="A1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}^{\text{equi}}(f)=\mathcal{L}(f)-\mathcal{L}({f}^{\text{equi}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mtext>equi</mtext></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>f</mi><mtext>equi</mtext></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}^{\text{equi}}(f)=\mathcal{L}(f)-\mathcal{L}({f}^{\text{equi}})</annotation></semantics></math> is non-negative and vanishes only when <math id="A1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is equivariant. This is a direct consequence of Jensen’s inequality applied to the strictly convex function <math id="A1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y\mapsto\ell(y,y^{\star})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">↦</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y\mapsto\ell(y,y^{\star})</annotation></semantics></math> (<a href="#S5.I1.i1" title="In 5.1 Optimality of target equivariant networks ‣ 5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">(A)</span></a>). Indeed, for any samples <math id="A1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(X,Y,X^{\star},Y^{\star})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>Y</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(X,Y,X^{\star},Y^{\star})</annotation></semantics></math>, the following holds:</span></p>
<table id="A1.EGx9" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A1.Ex3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\ell\left({f}^{\text{equi}}_{X,Y}\left(X^{\star}\right),Y^{\star}\right):" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><mtext>equi</mtext></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>Y</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo rspace="0.278em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\ell\left({f}^{\text{equi}}_{X,Y}\left(X^{\star}\right),Y^{\star}\right):</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\ell\left(\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\left[\sigma^{-1}\left(f_{X,\sigma(Y)}\left(X^{\star}\right)\right)\right],Y^{\star}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>Y</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\ell\left(\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\left[\sigma^{-1}\left(f_{X,\sigma(Y)}\left(X^{\star}\right)\right)\right],Y^{\star}\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="A1.Ex4"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\ell\left(\sigma^{-1}\left(f_{X,\sigma(Y)}\left(X^{\star}\right)\right),Y^{\star}\right)," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>Y</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\ell\left(\sigma^{-1}\left(f_{X,\sigma(Y)}\left(X^{\star}\right)\right),Y^{\star}\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.p3.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p3.2.1" class="ltx_text">where the first line follows by definition of <math id="A1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{f}^{\text{equi}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>f</mi><mtext>equi</mtext></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{f}^{\text{equi}}</annotation></semantics></math> while the second line uses Jensen’s inequality. Further taking the expectation w.r.t. <math id="A1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> shows that <math id="A1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}^{\text{equi}}(f)\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mtext>equi</mtext></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}^{\text{equi}}(f)\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math>. If <math id="A1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}^{\text{equi}}(f)=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mtext>equi</mtext></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}^{\text{equi}}(f)=0</annotation></semantics></math>, then by the above inequality it holds that <math id="A1.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell\left({f}^{\text{equi}}_{X,Y}\left(X^{\star}\right),Y^{\star}\right)=\ell\left(f_{X,Y}\left(X^{\star}\right),Y^{\star}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><mtext>equi</mtext></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>Y</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>Y</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell\left({f}^{\text{equi}}_{X,Y}\left(X^{\star}\right),Y^{\star}\right)=\ell\left(f_{X,Y}\left(X^{\star}\right),Y^{\star}\right)</annotation></semantics></math> almost surely. However, since <math id="A1.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> is strictly convex in its first argument (<a href="#S5.I1.i1" title="In 5.1 Optimality of target equivariant networks ‣ 5 Target permutation equivariance and prior-fitted networks ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">(A)</span></a>), the previous equality is only possible when <math id="A1.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{f}^{\text{equi}}=f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mtext>equi</mtext></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{f}^{\text{equi}}=f</annotation></semantics></math> almost surely, meaning that <math id="A1.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is equivariant.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text">Finally, to show the final result, we note that:</span></p>
