<p id="A1.p4.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p4.2.1" class="ltx_text">Here, the cross-product term equals <math id="A1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> since <math id="A1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\left[\sigma^{-1}\left(f_{X,\sigma(Y)}\left(X^{\star}\right)\right)\right]={f}^{\text{equi}}_{X,Y}\left(X^{\star}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><mtext>equi</mtext></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\left[\sigma^{-1}\left(f_{X,\sigma(Y)}\left(X^{\star}\right)\right)\right]={f}^{\text{equi}}_{X,Y}\left(X^{\star}\right)</annotation></semantics></math> by definition of <math id="A1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{f}^{\text{equi}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>f</mi><mtext>equi</mtext></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{f}^{\text{equi}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Hence, we have shown that:</span></p>
<table id="A1.EGx11" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A1.Ex11"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{E}^{\text{equi}}(f)=\mathbb{E}_{p}\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\left[\lVert\sigma^{-1}\left(f_{X,\sigma(Y)}\left(X^{\star}\right)\right)-{f}^{\text{equi}}_{X,Y}\left(X^{\star}\right)\rVert^{2}\right]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mtext>equi</mtext></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><msup><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><mtext>equi</mtext></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{E}^{\text{equi}}(f)=\mathbb{E}_{p}\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\left[\lVert\sigma^{-1}\left(f_{X,\sigma(Y)}\left(X^{\star}\right)\right)-{f}^{\text{equi}}_{X,Y}\left(X^{\star}\right)\rVert^{2}\right]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.p4.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p4.3.1" class="ltx_text">Finally, we use the invariance of the squared error to permutations, the equivariance of <math id="A1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{f}^{\text{equi}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>f</mi><mtext>equi</mtext></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{f}^{\text{equi}}</annotation></semantics></math> to permutations, and the invariance of <math id="A1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> to permutations to get:</span></p>
<table id="A1.EGx12" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A1.Ex12"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{E}^{\text{equi}}(f)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mtext>equi</mtext></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{E}^{\text{equi}}(f)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex12.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p}\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\left[\lVert f_{X,\sigma(Y)}\left(X^{\star}\right)-\sigma\left({f}^{\text{equi}}_{X,Y}\left(X^{\star}\right)\right)\rVert^{2}\right]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><msup><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><mtext>equi</mtext></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p}\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\left[\lVert f_{X,\sigma(Y)}\left(X^{\star}\right)-\sigma\left({f}^{\text{equi}}_{X,Y}\left(X^{\star}\right)\right)\rVert^{2}\right]</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Additional Experimental details</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Training procedure.</span>
We use a similar training protocol as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hollmann et al. [12]</a></cite>, in which the model is trained on classification datasets generated according to their proposed artificial dataset prior. In this protocol, each dataset has a fixed size of <math id="A2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1024" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1024</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1024</annotation></semantics></math> and is split into training and test uniformly at random. The maximum number of classes is fixed to <math id="A2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math>, while the maximum dimension of the covariate vector is fixed to <math id="A2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>100</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100</annotation></semantics></math>. Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Müller et al. [22]</a></cite>, we represent the target <math id="A2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> as a one-hot encoding vector whose dimension is the number of classes in the dataset. Moreover, we employ the exact same strategy for handling missing values in the covariates.
Training is performed using 153600 batches of 72 synthetically generated datasets each, which means the model was exposed to <math id="A2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>11M artificial datasets during pre-training, a similar order of magnitude of datasets used for pre-training TabPFN by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hollmann et al. [12]</a></cite>. The total training time of the network lasts approximately 4 days on a single A100 GPU with 80GB of GPU memory. The resulting network is then used for all our evaluations without altering its parameters.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We used the Adam optimizer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite> with initial learning rate of <math id="A2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.0001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.0001</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.0001</annotation></semantics></math> and linear-warmup scheduler for the first <math id="A2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math> epochs followed by cosine annealing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite> as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hollmann et al. [12]</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Architecture details.</span>
We use an EquiTabPFN network with <math id="A2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="12" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>12</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">12</annotation></semantics></math> self-attention layers alternating between both type of attention introduced in <a href="#S4" title="4 Target equivariant prior-fitted network ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>: 6 blocks <math id="A2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{SelfAtt}_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">SelfAtt</mtext><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{SelfAtt}_{c}</annotation></semantics></math> and 6 blocks <math id="A2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{SelfAtt}_{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">SelfAtt</mtext><mi>b</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{SelfAtt}_{b}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Each self-attention layer consists of a multi-head attention blocks with <math id="A2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math> heads, embeddings of dimension <math id="A2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="512" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>512</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">512</annotation></semantics></math>, and hidden layers of dimension <math id="A2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1024" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1024</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1024</annotation></semantics></math>.
This choice ensures a fair comparison with the models used in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hollmann et al. [12]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Müller et al. [22]</a></cite>, since the number of parameters (<math id="A2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="25.17M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>25.17</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">25.17M</annotation></semantics></math>) are of the same order when counting them as proposed in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaplan et al. [14]</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Datasets.</span> For the datasets with less than <math id="A2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math> classes, we collect the ones with less than <math id="A2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3000</annotation></semantics></math> samples and <math id="A2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>100</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100</annotation></semantics></math> features and retain the datasets that contain the same number of classes accross all folds and splits. For the datasets with more than <math id="A2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math> classes, we filter in addition the ones able to run inference on an 80GB A100 GPU. The datasets obtained are given in <a href="#A2.T1" title="In Appendix B Additional Experimental details ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and <a href="#A3.T5" title="In C.4 Critical difference diagrams and performance metric tables ‣ Appendix C Additional experiment results ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.</p>
</div>

<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Additional experiment results</h2>

<section id="A3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.1 </span>Ablation on the different components of EquiTabPFN.</h3>

<div id="A3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A3.T3" title="In C.1 Ablation on the different components of EquiTabPFN. ‣ Appendix C Additional experiment results ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> reports relative error reduction over TabPFN in two settings:
(1) <span id="A3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TabPFN bb + Eq dec.</span> using the TabPFN backbone (without bi-attention) and our equivariant decoder, and
(2) <span id="A3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bi-attn bb + MLP dec.</span> using a bi-attention backbone and a standard MLP decoder from TabPFNv1. Since the encoder is a simple linear embedding, it is considered part of the backbone: fully connected for TabPFN-style models and 1x1 convolution for biattention-based ones. The combination of both—biattention and the equivariant decoder, <span id="A3.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g</span>., the EquiTabPFN model we propose—yields the largest performance gain. We also tried using TabPFNv2 architecture backbone and modified it to make it target equivariant, then trained it using the publicly available code for the prior used for training TabPFNv1. This led to improvements compared to TabPFNv2<sup id="A3.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_sup">∗</sup> (the version we retrained ourselves using publicly available training prior). However, we found that using TabPFNv1’s backbone yielded the best performance overall.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.T3" class="ltx_table">
<table id="A3.T3.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="A3.T3.3.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A3.T3.3.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt"></th>
<td id="A3.T3.3.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="A3.T3.3.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">EquiTabPFN</span></td>
<td id="A3.T3.3.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="A3.T3.3.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TabPFN bb + Eq dec.</span></td>
<td id="A3.T3.3.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="A3.T3.3.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bi-attn bb + MLP dec.</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A3.T3.3.2" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A3.T3.3.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t"><span id="A3.T3.3.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">% Error reduction</span></th>
<td id="A3.T3.3.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t">+1.50%</td>
<td id="A3.T3.3.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t">+0.94%</td>
<td id="A3.T3.3.2.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t">-0.12%</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A3.T3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 3</span>: </span><span id="A3.T3.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Error reduction over TabPFN for different model configurations. </span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.2 </span>Computational cost comparisons</h3>

<div id="A3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Run time comparison.</span> <a href="#A3.T4" title="In C.2 Computational cost comparisons ‣ Appendix C Additional experiment results ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows the run time comparison between EquiTabPFN, TabPFNv1 and TabPFNv2 on both types of datasets (small or large number of classes).
On a small number of classes, EquiTabPFN incurs a slowdown of 5x compared to TabPFNv1. This is expected as TabPFNv1 was optimized to handle data with less than 10 classes.
On datasets with more than 10 classes, the gap narrows (only 1.3x slowdown) as TabPFNv1 requires ensembling techniques to handle the larger number of classes.
A more complete picture accounts for the tradeoff between time cost and performance as in <a href="#S6.F5" title="In 6.2 Main results ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> (left) and shows a clear advantage of EquiTabPFN in terms of efficiency.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.T4" class="ltx_table">
<table id="A3.T4.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="A3.T4.3.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A3.T4.3.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt"></th>
<th id="A3.T4.3.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="A3.T4.3.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">EquiTabPFN</span></th>
<th id="A3.T4.3.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="A3.T4.3.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TabPFNv1</span></th>
<th id="A3.T4.3.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="A3.T4.3.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TabPFNv2</span></th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="A3.T4.3.2" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A3.T4.3.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t"><span id="A3.T4.3.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">&lt; 10 Classes</span></th>
<td id="A3.T4.3.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">0.12</td>
<td id="A3.T4.3.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">0.02</td>
<td id="A3.T4.3.2.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">0.16</td></tr>
<tr id="A3.T4.3.3" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A3.T4.3.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_bb"><span id="A3.T4.3.3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">&gt; 10 Classes</span></th>
<td id="A3.T4.3.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">0.40</td>
<td id="A3.T4.3.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">0.30</td>
<td id="A3.T4.3.3.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">2.80</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A3.T4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 4</span>: </span><span id="A3.T4.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Time comparison (in seconds) across two types of datasets, depending on their class count.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">FLOPS comparaison.</span>
While EquiTabPFN and TabPFN have similar parameter counts, EquiTabPFN uses more FLOPS. On an A100 GPU with 2,000 samples (100 features, 10 classes), EquiTabPFN required 566 GFLOPS vs. 76 GFLOPS for TabPFN (<math id="A3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>7.45× more). However, with more classes (15), the gap narrows due to the ensembling needed for TabPFN to handle more than 10 classes (EquiTabPFN: 820 GFLOPS; TabPFN: 456 GFLOPS), consistent with runtime trends. Overall, those numbers remain small for a modern GPU given that a single H100 can easily reach 400 TFLOPS on an LLM training workflow for instance.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Memory cost.</span> EquiTabPFN incurs an increase compared to TabPFN which was translated in the use of smaller batch size (first dimension of the activation tensors). However, the context (in terms of the number of samples that can be processed by the model on our devices) was not affected in the experiments. This is likely due to the moderate size of the contexts used whose ranges are within the recommended limits for TabPFN.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.3 </span>Binary classification decision boundary</h3>

<div id="A3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In <a href="#A3.F6" title="In C.3 Binary classification decision boundary ‣ Appendix C Additional experiment results ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, we show the decision boundary on 3 binary classification datasets for multiple baselines. To illustrate the stability of the method, we do not do ensembling for TabPFN and EquiTabPFN.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.F6" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.06684v4/classification_boundary_comparison.svg" id="A3.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:467/156;" width="467" height="156"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A3.F6.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="A3.F6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Binary classification decision boundary for 7 methods on 3 datasets.
Even without ensembling, the boundary of EquiTabPFN is stable and smooth as opposed to TabPFN .</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.4 </span>Critical difference diagrams and performance metric tables</h3>

<div id="A3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We show the critical diagram using Autorank implementation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite> in <a href="#A3.F8" title="In C.4 Critical difference diagrams and performance metric tables ‣ Appendix C Additional experiment results ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> for datasets with more than 10 classes and <a href="#A3.F7" title="In C.4 Critical difference diagrams and performance metric tables ‣ Appendix C Additional experiment results ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> for datasets with less than 10 classes.
Critical diagrams show the average rank of each method (lower is better) and use a horizontal bar to show the methods statistically tied. We set the confidence level to <math id="A3.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.05</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.05</annotation></semantics></math> and use default hyper-parameters while forcing non-parametric mode to ensure stability.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We also give aggregate results for datasets with more than 10 classes in <a href="#A3.T5" title="In C.4 Critical difference diagrams and performance metric tables ‣ Appendix C Additional experiment results ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> and less than 10 classes in <a href="#A3.T6" title="In C.4 Critical difference diagrams and performance metric tables ‣ Appendix C Additional experiment results ‣ EquiTabPFN: A Target-Permutation Equivariant Prior Fitted Network" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.</p>
</div>
